knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))$, given that

$$
u=8 x\qquad v=y\qquad w=z.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation

$$
T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T$ is $\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}$.

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}$, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$.

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=8 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=1 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=8\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=8\left(1\cdot 1-0\right) \\ &=8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: x,y,z real; nonzero constant inverse determinant

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}4\left({e}^{x}\right) \\ 2\left({e}^{x+y}\right) \\ 2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=4\left({e}^{x}\right),\,v(x,y,z)=2\left({e}^{x+y}\right),\,w(x,y,z)=2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =4\left({e}^{x}\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2\left({e}^{x+y}\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2\left({e}^{x+y}\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $4, 2, 2$ multiplies the determinant by $16$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4\left({e}^{x}\right) & 0 & 0 \\ 2\left({e}^{x+y}\right) & 2\left({e}^{x+y}\right) & 0 \\ 2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right) & 2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right) & 2\left({e}^{x+y+z}\right)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =16\left({e}^{x}\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{x+y} & 0 \\ {e}^{x+y+z} & {e}^{x+y+z}\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =16\left({e}^{x}({e}^{2x+2y+z}-0)\right)\\  & =16 e^{x} e^{x + y} e^{x + y + z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}16\left({e}^{3x+2y+z}\right) & =16\left({e}^{x+(x+y)+(x+y+z)}\right) \\  & =16\left({e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{x+y}\cdot {e}^{x+y+z}\right) \\  & =16\left(\left(\frac{u}{4}\right)\left(\frac{v}{2}\right)\left(\frac{w}{2}\right)\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{u v w}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}4\left(x\right) \\ 2\left(z-y\right) \\ 2\left(xy\right)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=4\left(x\right),\,v(x,y,z)=2\left(z-y\right),\,w(x,y,z)=2\left(xy\right).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =4\left(1\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2\left(-1\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =2\left(1\right) \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2\left(y\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2\left(x\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $4, 2, 2$ multiplies the determinant by $16$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4\left(1\right) & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\left(-1\right) & 2\left(1\right) \\ 2\left(y\right) & 2\left(x\right) & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =16\left(1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ x & 0\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =16\left(1(0-x)\right)\\  & =- 16 x.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}16\left(-x\right) & =16\left(-\left(\frac{u}{4}\right)\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}\left(\frac{1}{(-\left(\frac{u}{4}\right))}\right) \\  & =- \frac{1}{4 u}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}4\left(xy\right) \\ 2\left(yz\right) \\ 2\left(xz\right)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=4\left(xy\right),\,v(x,y,z)=2\left(yz\right),\,w(x,y,z)=2\left(xz\right).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =4\left(y\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =4\left(x\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2\left(z\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =2\left(y\right) \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2\left(z\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =2\left(x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $4, 2, 2$ multiplies the determinant by $16$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4\left(y\right) & 4\left(x\right) & 0 \\ 0 & 2\left(z\right) & 2\left(y\right) \\ 2\left(z\right) & 0 & 2\left(x\right)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =16\left(y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =16\left(y(xz-0)-x(0-yz)\right)\\  & =16\left(xyz+xyz\right)\\  & =32 x y z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}16\left(2xyz\right) & =16\left(2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}}\right) \\  & =16\left(2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}\right) \\  & =16\left(2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)}\right) \\  & =16\left(2\sqrt{\left(\frac{u}{4}\right)\left(\frac{v}{2}\right)\left(\frac{w}{2}\right)}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8 \sqrt{u v w}}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}4\left(y{z}^{2}\right) \\ 2\left(z{x}^{2}\right) \\ 2\left(x{y}^{2}\right)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=4\left(y{z}^{2}\right),\,v(x,y,z)=2\left(z{x}^{2}\right),\,w(x,y,z)=2\left(x{y}^{2}\right).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =4\left({z}^{2}\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =4\left(2yz\right) \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2\left(2xz\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =2\left({x}^{2}\right) \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2\left({y}^{2}\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2\left(2xy\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $4, 2, 2$ multiplies the determinant by $16$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4\left({z}^{2}\right) & 4\left(2yz\right) \\ 2\left(2xz\right) & 0 & 2\left({x}^{2}\right) \\ 2\left({y}^{2}\right) & 2\left(2xy\right) & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =16\left(-{z}^{2}\begin{vmatrix}2xz & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{vmatrix}+2yz\begin{vmatrix}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =16\left(-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0)\right)\\  & =16\left({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\right)\\  & =144 x^{2} y^{2} z^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}16\left(9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\right) & =16\left(9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3}\right) \\  & =16\left(9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3}\right) \\  & =16\left(9(\left(\frac{u}{4}\right)\left(\frac{v}{2}\right)\left(\frac{w}{2}\right))^{2/3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{2^{\frac{2}{3}}}{36 \left(u v w\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}4\left(\frac{z}{y}\right) \\ 2\left(y\right) \\ 2\left(xz\right)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $y,z\ne 0.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=4\left(\frac{z}{y}\right),\,v(x,y,z)=2\left(y\right),\,w(x,y,z)=2\left(xz\right).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =4\left(-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}}\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =4\left(\frac{1}{y}\right) \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2\left(1\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2\left(z\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =2\left(x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $4, 2, 2$ multiplies the determinant by $16$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4\left(-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}}\right) & 4\left(\frac{1}{y}\right) \\ 0 & 2\left(1\right) & 0 \\ 2\left(z\right) & 0 & 2\left(x\right)\end{vmatrix} \\  & =16\left(z\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y} \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =16\left(z(0-\frac{1}{y})\right)\\  & =- \frac{16 z}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}4\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \\ 2\left(\sqrt{y}+z\right) \\ 2\left({y}^{2}\right)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=4\left(\frac{1}{x}\right),\,v(x,y,z)=2\left(\sqrt{y}+z\right),\,w(x,y,z)=2\left({y}^{2}\right).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =4\left(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\right) & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =2\left(1\right) \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2\left(2y\right) & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $4, 2, 2$ multiplies the determinant by $16$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4\left(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\right) & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\right) & 2\left(1\right) \\ 0 & 2\left(2y\right) & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =16\left(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =\frac{32 y}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}16\left(\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}\right) & =16\left(\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{{y}^{2}}\right) \\  & =16\left({\left(\frac{u}{4}\right)}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{\left(\frac{w}{2}\right)}\right) \\  & =16\left(2{\left(\frac{u}{4}\right)}^{2}\sqrt{\left(\frac{w}{2}\right)}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2 u^{2} \sqrt{w}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))$, given that

$$
u=5 x\qquad v=8 y\qquad w=z.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation

$$
T:(u,v,w)\to(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T$ is $\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}$.

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}$, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$.

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=5 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}=8 & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z}=0 \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}=0 & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}&=\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=5\begin{vmatrix}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=5\left(8\cdot 1-0\right) \\ &=40\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{1}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

question.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=2\left(2x+y\right),\,v=-x+3y-2z,\,w=3y+4z.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2\left(2\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =2\left(1\right) & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =-2 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Scaling the three derivative rows by $2, 1, 1$ multiplies the determinant by $2$.

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2\left(2\right) & 2\left(1\right) & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\left(2\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\right)\\  & =2\left(2(12+6)-1(-4-0)\right)\\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{80}.\end{aligned}
$$
